issues.subcategory: Sample description contradiction
issues.description: The Methods section describes participants as recruited through the 'introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington' with an average age of 19 years and 68% female, yet the Abstract, Introduction, Discussion, and Conclusion repeatedly describe this as a 'national probability sample' or 'nationally representative sample.' A university student convenience sample is fundamentally different from a national probability sample. The paper also references the NZAVS (New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study), which is a national probability sample, but the participant description clearly indicates a student sample. This is a critical contradiction that undermines the entire framing and generalizability claims of the paper.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013). Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.subcategory: False claim of national representativeness
issues.description: The Discussion states 'Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.' This is directly contradicted by the Methods section, which describes a student sample from a single university with N=374, average age 19, 68% female, and 86% Pākehā. This is not nationally representative by any standard definition. The entire theoretical contribution of the paper rests on extending findings from student samples to the general population, yet the sample described is itself a student sample.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.subcategory: Mismatch between stated and measured construct
issues.description: The Abstract and much of the paper describe the outcome variable as 'willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment' or 'willingness to sacrifice for the environment,' but the Measures section describes only two items measuring environmental concern ('How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'). These items measure concern/beliefs, not willingness to change behavior or make sacrifices. The construct as operationalized does not match the construct as described throughout the paper.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, "How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?" and "To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?".

issues.subcategory: Implausible chi-square difference test value
issues.description: The chi-square difference test comparing the bidirectional associations between SDO and RWA yields χ²(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001. A chi-square difference value of over 15,000 with 1 degree of freedom is extraordinarily large and implausible for a sample of 374 participants. This likely reflects a computational or reporting error. For comparison, the other chi-square difference tests in the same analysis yield values of 2.34, 39.97, and 2.70, making this value approximately 4,000 times larger than the next largest value.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.subcategory: Contradictory interpretation of non-significant difference test
issues.description: The chi-square difference test comparing SDO vs. RWA as predictors of environmentalism was non-significant (χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126), meaning the constrained model (assuming equal paths) fits comparably to the unconstrained model. Despite this, the authors conclude that 'SDO is a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA.' A non-significant difference test means there is insufficient evidence to claim one predictor is statistically stronger than the other, directly contradicting the paper's central claim.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.subcategory: Inadequate measurement - two-item scale
issues.description: Environmentalism is measured with only two items, one of which is reverse-coded. No reliability estimate is reported for this two-item measure. With only two items, the construct is likely measured with substantial error, and the content validity of the measure is questionable. Furthermore, one item asks about concern and the other about exaggeration of environmental problems—these may tap different constructs.
issues.quote: "How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?" and "To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?"

issues.subcategory: Confidence intervals inconsistent with sample size
issues.description: The confidence intervals reported in Table 1 are extremely narrow (e.g., SDO mean = 2.60 [2.58, 2.63], SD = .96 [.95, .98]). For a sample of N = 374, the 95% CI for a mean of 2.60 with SD = 0.96 should be approximately [2.50, 2.70] (±0.097). The reported CI width of 0.05 would require a sample size of approximately 14,000+. This suggests either the CIs are computed on a much larger sample than the 374 reported, or there is an error in the reported sample size or confidence intervals.

issues.subcategory: Chi-square model fit inconsistent with sample size
issues.description: The overall model chi-square is reported as χ²(2279) = 36511.73. For a sample of N = 374, this chi-square to df ratio (~16:1) is extremely high and the absolute value seems implausibly large for this sample size. Chi-square values of this magnitude typically arise from much larger samples (thousands of participants). This further suggests the analyses may have been conducted on a different (larger) dataset than the N = 374 student sample described in the Methods.

issues.subcategory: Model fit below acceptable thresholds
issues.description: The CFI of .86 is below the conventional threshold of .90 (and well below the more stringent .95 threshold). The authors dismiss this by attributing it to model complexity, but poor CFI indicates meaningful misfit. Accepting a model with CFI = .86 while selectively relying on RMSEA and SRMR represents cherry-picking fit indices. The SRMR of .07 is also only marginally acceptable (threshold typically .08). The poor CFI suggests the model may not adequately represent the data.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07)

issues.subcategory: Inappropriate causal claims from cross-lagged panel model
issues.description: The authors make causal claims based on a cross-lagged panel model (e.g., 'These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism'). However, cross-lagged panel models do not establish causation. They are subject to well-documented limitations including the inability to separate between-person and within-person effects, sensitivity to measurement intervals, and confounding by stable unmeasured third variables. The authors acknowledge third-variable explanations briefly but still make causal claims throughout.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism. The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance

issues.subcategory: Missing standardized coefficients
issues.description: The authors state 'We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances,' but Figure 1 reportedly shows unstandardized parameters. The standardized coefficients are not presented anywhere in the text or tables, making it impossible to assess effect sizes in standardized metric or compare across paths in a meaningful way.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances.

issues.subcategory: Missing reliability for environmentalism measure
issues.description: Table 1 reports reliabilities for SDO (.69) and RWA (.70) but the reliability reported for the environmentalism measure (.76) is not discussed in context. More importantly, with only two items, Cronbach's alpha is equivalent to the Spearman-Brown corrected correlation, and the appropriateness of this reliability estimate for a two-item scale should be discussed. Additionally, reliabilities at other time points are not reported.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.subcategory: Missing item in RWA scale at one time point
issues.description: One of the six RWA items was not assessed at Time 2, meaning the RWA measure differs across time points. This creates a measurement invariance problem that is not addressed. The authors do not discuss how this was handled in the analysis or whether it affects the comparability of RWA scores across time points.
issues.quote: The item "Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done", was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.subcategory: Listwise deletion with likely substantial attrition
issues.description: The authors use listwise deletion across five time points. With a student sample tracked over five years (from introductory psychology), attrition is likely substantial, but no information is provided about retention rates, dropout patterns, or whether those who dropped out differ systematically from those who remained. Listwise deletion can introduce severe bias if data are not missing completely at random (MCAR), and with longitudinal data spanning five years of a student sample, MCAR is implausible.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.subcategory: Missing attrition information
issues.description: No information is provided about how many participants were initially recruited, how many dropped out at each wave, or the characteristics of those who dropped out versus those who remained. The authors refer readers to the NZAVS website for details, but this information is essential for evaluating the study and should be in the manuscript.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent significance threshold
issues.description: The Methods section states 'we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings,' but Figure 1's caption states 'All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.' These are contradictory thresholds. Additionally, the rationale for adopting p < .05 'because of the large sample size' is backwards—large samples typically warrant more stringent thresholds, not the standard one.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.subcategory: Cross-lagged panel model without random intercept
issues.description: The authors use a traditional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) without accounting for stable between-person differences (i.e., no random intercept cross-lagged panel model, RI-CLPM). Hamaker et al. (2015) demonstrated that traditional CLPMs conflate between-person and within-person effects, potentially leading to spurious cross-lagged effects. Given that SDO, RWA, and environmentalism likely have stable trait-like components, the failure to separate these levels of analysis is a significant limitation.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction with previous study's sample characterization
issues.description: The Introduction criticizes Stanley et al. [14] for using a student sample and frames the current study as advancing this work by using a 'general population sample.' However, the Methods section describes what appears to be a student sample (introductory psychology pool, mean age 19). The entire rationale for the study—that the SDO-environmentalism link is stronger in general population samples—is undermined if this is also a student sample.
issues.quote: We expand on Stanley et al.'s study by using a large, national probability sample spanning five years to examine how these variables relate over time in the general population.

issues.subcategory: Redundant constraint description
issues.description: The Data Analysis section describes constraining cross-lagged associations twice in identical language, suggesting a copy-paste error. This raises concerns about the care taken in manuscript preparation and whether the actual constraints applied are accurately described.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.subcategory: Missing descriptive statistics for later time points
issues.description: Descriptive statistics are only presented for Time 1. For a five-wave longitudinal study, descriptive statistics at each time point (or at minimum, means and SDs) are needed to evaluate trends, assess measurement properties over time, and understand the data. Correlations between variables across time points are also not reported.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration or alternative model testing
issues.description: There is no mention of pre-registration. The authors impose a stationary cross-lagged model with time-invariant parameters but do not test whether this constraint is justified (e.g., by comparing to a model with freely estimated parameters). The choice of constraints and model specification represents researcher degrees of freedom that could influence results.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.subcategory: Reporting SD instead of SE for parameter estimates
issues.description: The cross-lagged path coefficients are reported with 'SD' values (e.g., 'B = -.11, SD = .01'). For regression/path coefficients, the appropriate measure of uncertainty is the standard error (SE), not the standard deviation. This appears to be a labeling error, but it creates ambiguity about what is actually being reported.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.subcategory: Item-level path analysis without latent variables
issues.description: The description of constraining 'residual variance for the same item over time' suggests item-level path analysis rather than latent variable modeling. Using observed composite scores or item-level paths without latent variables fails to account for measurement error, which can bias cross-lagged estimates. Given the modest reliabilities (.69-.76), measurement error is non-trivial and could substantially attenuate or distort the cross-lagged paths.
issues.quote: We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.

issues.subcategory: Sample size described as 'large' but N=374
issues.description: The authors describe their dataset as having a 'large sample size' to justify their significance threshold, but N=374 is modest for a cross-lagged panel model with three constructs across five time points, especially when using listwise deletion. This is inconsistent with the NZAVS, which typically has tens of thousands of participants, further suggesting confusion about which dataset was actually analyzed.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent interpretation of RWA-SDO temporal relationship
issues.description: The finding that RWA predicts SDO but not vice versa is interpreted as suggesting 'New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.' This interpretation is non-sequitur: if RWA predicts increases in SDO, this would suggest that authoritarianism drives social dominance, not that people are 'socialized into authoritarianism.' The logic of the interpretation is reversed.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander's are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.subcategory: Missing autoregressive path coefficients
issues.description: The autoregressive (stability) paths are described as showing variables are 'relatively stable over time' but no numerical values are provided in the text. These coefficients are important for interpreting the cross-lagged effects and assessing the degree of rank-order stability.
issues.quote: As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time, consistent with our prediction that these variables remain largely unchanged over the study period.

issues.subcategory: Confidence interval inconsistency for RWA path
issues.description: The confidence interval for the RWA to environmentalism path is reported as [-.05, -.01], but the point estimate is B = -.02. While -.02 falls within this interval, the interval is notably asymmetric around the point estimate (extending .03 below but only .01 above), which is unusual for normally distributed parameter estimates.

issues.subcategory: NZAVS reference incomplete
issues.description: Reference 26 (Sibley C. New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study) is incomplete—it lacks a year, URL, or any identifying information that would allow readers to locate the referenced materials about sample details, procedure, and retention.
issues.quote: Sibley C. New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study.

issues.subcategory: No measurement invariance testing
issues.description: The authors do not test for measurement invariance across the five time points. Given that one RWA item was missing at Time 2 and that the study spans five years, establishing that the constructs are measured equivalently across time is essential for valid interpretation of cross-lagged effects.
issues.quote: The item "Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done", was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.
